## CHAPTER 14

## Dermatology

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Normal skin anatomy
- Dermatologic pharmacology concepts
- Skin infections: bacterial, viral, fungal
- Bites: human, animal, insects
- Dermatitis
- Primary, secondary, and malignant skin lesions
- Systemic conditions
- Dermatologic emergencies

## NOTES

- Three layers

- $ Epidermis: barrier
- $ Dermis: handles tensile load and contains nerves
- $ Hypodermis: insulation, energy, and fluid storage

<!-- image -->

## Dermatology: Terms to Know

Abscess: deep infection, localized collection of pus

Furuncle/boil: deep infection of hair follicles

Bulla or blister: fluid-filled or pus-filled >0.5 cm

Macule: flat change in skin with a color change (brown, blue, red, or hypopigmented)

Nodule: solid lesion >0.5-2.0 cm (nodule >2.0 cm is a tumor)

Papule: raised, solid lesion ≤0.5 cm; varies in color

Plaque: raised, solid lesion >0.5 cm

Vesicle: ≤0.5 cm elevated lesion that contains fluid

Wheal (hive): transient rounded or flat-top plaque

## Approach to Dermatology

- Understand the skin anatomy
- $ What layer is affected?
- $ OLD CARTS
- Pattern recognition!
- $ Physical exam findings
- Texture, plane, depth, color, borders, shape, blanching, distribution
- $ Consider: skin problem vs. systemic problem

TIP: Document an accurate, detailed description so that other clinicians can "see" the lesion by reading your notes! (See supplemental info.)

<!-- image -->

## ANATOMY OF THE SKIN

## Pharmacology and Skin

Choose the appropriate drug route

- Topical
- Systemic (Oral or IV)
- Supportive care: Not every condition needs medication!
- And when you don't know what to do:

"If it's wet, make it dry. If it's dry, make it wet."

## Skin Infections

- What causes them?
- $ Bacteria: Gram + organisms
- Usually Staph or Strep
- $ Fungi: two main types
- Dermatophytes: Tinea
- Candida
- $ Tinea versicolor (caused by yeast)
- $ Viruses: Many!
- Herpes, HPV, molluscum contagiosum, HIV, plantar warts, varicella, viral exanthems
- $ Infestations (parasites)

## Impetigo

- Superficial bacterial infection caused by Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, or both
- Classic description: "honey-colored crusts"
- Treat topically

## Cellulitis

- Bacterial infection of the dermis and hypodermis
- $ Group A Streptococcus
- $ Staphylococcus aureus
- Symptoms: erythema, edema, tender, warmth, possibly fever, elevated WBC count
- Nonpurulent cellulitis treatment:
- $ Oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin/ clavulanate, clindamycin

TIP: Deep, nonpurulent infection + systemic symptoms = systemic antibiotics!

## NOTES Bacterial Skin Infections

| Infection                                   | Usual Organism                  | Treatment per IDSA                                                                                                                    |
|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cellulitis w/o purulence                    | MSSA, Strep                     | Cephalexin, cefadroxil, clindamycin                                                                                                   |
| Cellulitis w/ purulence                     | MRSA                            | I & D first-line, TMP-SMX, clindamycin, tetracycline, linezolid (5 to 10 days)                                                        |
| Carbuncle (deep furuncle/boil) and abscess  | Staph (MRSA)                    | I & D first-line! Antibiotics if fever, +cellulitis >2.5cm, systemic sx, or failed initial tx                                         |
| Impetigo (superficial)                      | Strep, MSSA, or both!           | Mupirocin (Bactroban) or retapamulin (Altabax) BID ×5 days                                                                            |
| Ecthyma (deep, ulcerative form of impetigo) | MSSA (most common), MRSA, Strep | MSSA: dicloxacillin, cephalexin MRSA: doxycycline, clindamycin, or TMP-SMX                                                            |
| Folliculitis                                | MSSA                            | Topical: mupirocin or clindamycin gel Oral: cephalexin, dicloxacillin 4 ×/day MRSA: doxycycline or TMP-SMX Pseudomonas: ciprofloxacin |

## Bites: Human and Animal

## CAN LEAD TO BACTERIAL INFECTION!

Infection sources:

1. Oral flora of biter
2. $ Dog/cat: Pasteurella
3. $ Human: Staphylococcus/Streptococcus/anaerobes
2. Skin flora of the patient
5. $ Staphylococcus, Streptococcus most common

Antibiotic treatment:

- $ Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin)

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #8

A patient was bitten on the arm by a pet dog and has a superficial 1.5-cm simple laceration. How should this be managed?

1. Copious irrigation
2. Prophylactic antibiotics
3. Suture closure
4. Debridement

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Management of Bites

Clean and irrigate

Antibiotic prophylaxis

- Amoxicillin/clavulanate for 3 to 5 days if:
- $ Immunocompromised
- $ Suture closure
- $ Involvement of bones, joints, hands, face, or genitals
- $ Deep puncture wounds
- $ Human bites
- Tetanus prophylaxis if >5 years

## Management of Bites

Rabies prophylaxis indications:

## Animals:

- $ High-risk (skunks, raccoons, foxes, bats)
- $ Behaving atypically aggressive (squirrels, beavers)
- $ Cannot be obtained for testing
- $ Vaccination status unknown
- Refer emergently for:
- $ Rabies Immunoglobin (HRIG)
- $ Rabies Immunization (Rabivert): multidose series
- Reportable condition

## QUESTION #9

A patient was inadvertently bitten on the arm when trying to pet a raccoon. Following irrigation of the wound, what is the next step in management of this patient?

1. Suture the wound and follow up in 2 days for wound check.
2. Bandage the wound and provide education on signs and symptoms of infection.
3. Refer the patient to the emergency department for rabies prophylaxis.
4. Prescribe prophylactic amoxicillin/clavulanate for 3 to 5 days.

## Fungal Rashes

Dermatophyte

- Filamentous fungi
- Pruritic, scaling border, spreads centrifugally
- Named by location
- $ Capitis: scalp/hair
- $ Corporis: body
- $ Cruris: crural fold (groin)
- $ Unguium: nails

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES Candida

- Yeast
- Pruritic, erythematous base, white patches, burning, satellite lesions
- Named by location
- $ Oropharyngeal
- $ Vaginitis
- $ Balanitis
- $ Invasive

Which of the following fungal infections should not be treated with a topical antifungal?

1. Tinea corporis

## Viral Rashes

- Viral exanthems: characteristic skin lesions associated with viruses (e.g., measles, rubella, varicella)
- Viral enanthems: oral eruption preceding, occurring simultaneously or following an exanthem (i.e., Koplik spots in measles)
- Other viruses with skin manifestations:
- $ Common viruses
- HPV: common warts, plantar warts
- Molluscum contagiosum: 2- to 5-mm umbilicated papules
- Herpes simplex virus: two types (HSV1 and HSV2)
- Herpes zoster: shingles
- $ Sexually transmitted
- Human papilloma virus (HPV): genital warts
- Genital herpes simplex
- HIV: acute exanthem, infectious/neoplastic conditions

## Herpes Zoster Management

- Very painful condition, prodrome
- $ NSAIDs: mild to moderate pain
- $ Narcotics: for severe pain
- Antiviral therapy:
- $ <72 hours since onset:
- Oral acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir, or brivudine for 7 days
- $ >72 hours since onset:
- New lesions are appearing (ongoing viral replication)
- Immunocompromised

<!-- image -->

TIP: If patient is immunocompromised, ALWAYS prescribe antiviral therapy regardless of time since onset.

## Herpes Zoster Complications

| Complication               | Symptoms/Management                                                        |
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Ramsay Hunt syndrome       | Otologic: ear pain, vesicles, ipsilateral facial paralysis Referral to ENT |
| Postherpetic neuralgia     | Herpetic pain more than 4 months/same dermatome                            |
| Herpes zoster Ophthalmicus | Refer to ophthalmology urgently.                                           |
| Meningitis/Encephalitis    | Send to emergency department.                                              |

## QUESTION #13

A 51-year-old is being treated today for herpes zoster. The patient asks when they can receive the shingles vaccine. Which of the following statements is true?

1. The patient requires testing for serologic evidence of varicella.
2. Shingrix should not be given if the patient has received Zostavax.
3. Administer the vaccine to the patient today.
4. Vaccine can be given upon resolution of acute episode of herpes zoster.

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Shingles Prevention Recombinant Zoster Vaccine (RZV): Shingrix

- CDC recommendations:
- $ Immunocompetent patients ≥50 years
- $ Immunocompromised patients ≥19 years
- $ 2 IM injections given 2 to 6 months apart
- For immunocompromised patients, may give 1 to 2 months apart (if immunodeficient, immunosuppressed)
- Shingrix is a recombinant vaccine.
- $ Safer, higher efficacy than Zostavax (a live vaccine)
- $ Administer without regard to Zostavax history.

## Insect Bites: Spiders

Bites inject toxins that cause swelling and inflammation; some spider bites cause tissue necrosis or systemic neurologic symptoms.

- Single lesion, definitive diagnosis requires visualization of the spider.
- Not experienced by multiple members of household

brown recluse bite image

<!-- image -->

TIP: Spider bites often mistaken for MRSA abscesses, herpes zoster, Lyme disease

## Insect Bites: Ticks

## SYMPTOMS

2 to 14 days post exposure

- Requires ~36 hours contact for disease transmission
- Skin eruption varies among tick species
- Lyme disease transmitted most often; others-Rocky mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis

Lyme Disease: Erythema migrans (bull's eye rash)

<!-- image -->

Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever: Diffuse lesions includes palms of hands and soles of feet

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #14

A 34-year-old female presents reporting a bite from a tick that she removed yesterday. Which of the following statements are true?

1. Erythema migrans may take up to 120 days to appear.
2. Antibiotic prophylaxis should be initiated for all ticks removed.
3. Prophylaxis should be initiated within 12 hours of tick removal.
4. A single dose of doxycycline is preferred prophylaxis.

<!-- image -->

## Insect Bites: Ticks

## Treatment

Doxycycline 100 mg BID × 10 d OR Amoxicillin OR Cefuroxime

*Doxycycline is the only recommended treatment for RMSF.

## Insect Bites: Bed Bugs

- Erythematous papule (2-5 mm), pruritic
- Reaction: varies, immediate up to 10 days

<!-- image -->

## PEP

Doxycycline 200 mg single dose (peds:4.4 mg/kg)

*PEP not recommended for RMSF

- 1 week resolution, untreated
- Diagnosis requires detection of bed bugs

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## PEP checklist:

- Endemic area
- Tick removed within 72 hours
- Engorged
- Ixodes tick
- Doxy is safe

## NOTES

## NOTES

## Insect Bites: Scabies

Mite Infestation (Sarcoptes Scabiei)

- 3 to 6 weeks for symptoms to appear
- Skin-to-skin transmission
- Not animals-to-humans
- Intensely pruritic lesions, small erythematous papules with burrows
- Distribution: sides/webs of fingers, wrist, axillae, areola, genitalia, waist

## Treatment

- Topical permethrin cream
- $ Safe for age >2 months and in pregnancy/lactating
- $ Applied to entire body (except head) once, can repeat in 2 weeks

<!-- image -->

## Insect Bites: Pediculosis (Lice)

- Distribution:
- $ Head (capitis): most common
- $ Body (corporis)
- $ Pubic hair (pubis): sexually transmitted
- Treatment:
- $ Topical permethrin or malathion
- $ Wet combing with proper technique q 3-4 days for at least 3 weeks is a reasonable alternative

<!-- image -->

## Dermatitis

Eczema

## TOPICAL STEROID CHARACTERISTICS

- Topical steroids work by causing vasoconstriction.
- Two concepts:
- $ Potency: amount of drug needed to produce effect; affected by the amount of vasoconstriction produced, immunosuppressive effects, and the vehicle used
- $ Vehicle: medium that contains the medicine

<!-- image -->

| Vehicle   | Considerations for Use                                               |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Ointment  | Works well in thick or hyperkeratotic lesions; avoid in hairy areas  |
| Cream     | Less residue, dries quickly; use in skinfolds and acute inflammation |
| Lotion    | Works well in hairy areas; less occlusive, dries quickly             |
| Gel       | Works in hairy areas, especially scalp (nongreasy)                   |
| Foam      | Ideal for scalps, but expensive                                      |

## NOTES

## NOTES Skin Tumors

- Benign
- $ Seborrheic keratosis
- $ Skin tags
- $ Polyps
- $ Cysts

$ Lipoma

- $ Many more
- Premalignant
- $ Actinic keratosis
- Malignant
- $ Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)
- $ Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
- $ Melanoma

## Skin Lesion Evaluation

- Visual inspection:
- $ Asymmetry (one half does not match the other half)
- $ Border (irregular, not smooth)
- $ Color (more than one color in the same lesion)
- $ Diameter (more than 6 mm, pencil eraser)
- $ Evolving (changes in a mole)
- Refer: lesions highly suspicious for malignancy
- Punch/Shave biopsy: lesions of uncertain etiology, low suspicion for malignancy

## Seborrheic Keratosis

- Benign brown, warty lesion
- $ Usually found on the chest, back, or scalp
- $ "Stuck on" appearance
- $ May become irritated and bleed
- $ May be few or numerous lesions, cosmetic concerns
- Management
- $ Symptomatic lesions
- Cryotherapy
- Curettage/shave excision
- Electrodessication
- $ Biopsy suspicious lesions

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Actinic (Solar) Keratosis

- Scaling macules, papules, or plaques in sun-exposed areas
- $ Precancerous
- $ May progress to squamous cell carcinoma; no way to predict if it will or it won't
- Management
- $ Destructive therapies (liquid nitrogen cryosurgery; shave excision)
- $ Topicals (fluorouracil, imiquimod)
- Refer for Biopsy if:
- $ Indurated lesions
- $ Painful, ulcerated, or bleeding lesions
- $ Hyperkeratotic or hypertrophic actinic keratosis not resolving with standard therapy or recuring

<!-- image -->

1. Squamous cell carcinoma

## NOTES

## SKIN CANCERS

<!-- image -->

## Name That Skin Cancer

- Pink-red, flesh colored, nodular, telangiectasia, may be scaly
- Common on shoulders, chest, face, back
- Light skin
- Sun exposure, tanning beds, genetic predisposition

## Name That Skin Cancer

- Lesions vary, "plaque," crusting, ulceration, bleeding; flesh toned to erythemic
- Common on face, neck, scalp, extremities
- Sun exposure, actinic keratosis

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Name That Skin Cancer

- "Ugly Duckling Lesion" different than other nevi
- Violates the ABCDE rules-especially if changing, >6 mm
- Sensory change/itch inflammation
- Common on legs, upper back, sun exposed areas
- Brown/black longitudinal nail unit (great toe, thumb)
- Family history, tanning bed use, sun exposure

<!-- image -->

Multisystem autoimmune disease

## QUESTION #18

Which of the following is a required component of the diagnostic criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus?

1. Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
2. Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test
3. Presence of malar rash
4. Positive of antiphospholipid antibodies test

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Dermatologic Emergencies

If you see these, refer ASAP!

- Erysipelas: well-demarcated bright red rash with raised edges in a toxic-looking patient; caused by Streptococcus pyogenes
- Necrotizing fasciitis: rare, rapidly progressing skin infection; red/purple skin, severe pain and fever, necrosis of affected area

## Erysipelas

<!-- image -->

## Dermatologic Emergencies

Steven-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis:

- Severe mucocutaneous reaction resulting in extensive necrosis and detachment of epidermis
- $ Caused by: medication or infection
- Prodrome: fever >102°F (38.9°C), flu-like symptoms 1 to 3 days
- Mucocutaneous lesions
- $ Target lesions with central dusky purpura
- $ Maybe bullae and blister formation
- $ Spreads from face downward
- $ May include positive Nikolsky sign (exfoliation of skin with rubbing)

Steven Johnson Syndrome: Mucous membranes

<!-- image -->

- Diseases/conditions that present with
- Vesicles/bulla
